info.desc: Antichrist Superstar is the second studio album by American rock band Marilyn Manson, released on October 8, 1996, by Nothing and Interscope Records. It was recorded at Nothing Studios in New Orleans and produced by the band's eponymous vocalist along with Sean Beavan, former Skinny Puppy producer Dave Ogilvie and Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails. The recording of the album was marred by excessive drug use, which provoked a high level of antagonism between band members. Consequently, it was their last release to feature contributions from founding guitarist Daisy Berkowitz, who acrimoniously quit partway through recording. .

podcast.body: Marilyn Manson's album *Antichrist Superstar* was re-issued on cassette for Cassette Store Day, despite not having an original cassette release during its initial run. The re-issue, typically priced around 9 euros, raised concerns about its audio quality due to the low cost, suggesting it wasn't made with premium tape. podcast.body: Musically, "Antichrist Superstar" is a complex piece, incorporating classic rock, goth metal, industrial rock, progressive music, progressive metal, and elements of new wave and synthesizers, making it one of the most complex albums in rock history. It remains a key album for understanding the evolution of rock over the last 30-40 years, despite many people not delving into it due to bad press. "Musicalmente este álbum es la leche, es complejísimo, de los álbumes más complejos que había en la historia del rock."

podcast.body: Released in 1996, this album is the last chronological part of a conceptual trilogy that forms Manson's autobiography told in reverse order. It features a three-part storyline chronicling the rise of the Antichrist Superstar, a Nietzschean character who sheds his humanity and becomes a "pretty awful dude." "Antichrist Superstar, from 1996, has a three-part storyline that follows the rise of, well, the Antichrist Superstar, a Nietzschean character who, after shedding the remnants of his humanity, turns out to be a pretty awful dude."

podcast.body: Released in 1996, this album represents a major artistic leap for Marilyn Manson, with a complex and philosophical argument. It was produced by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails and co-produced by Sean Beavan, involving many collaborators from Nine Inch Nails. The album's themes and inspiration were developed in 1995, followed by a six-month recording process in early 1996. "el anticristo superestar va mucho más allá."

podcast.body: The album stands out for its exceptionally high level of aggression, its deeply macabre themes, and the profound impact it had on both the music industry and society at large. "Destinde mucho el nivel de agresividad y sobre todo el nivel de como de macabro es y de impactación."

podcast.body: The music videos associated with "Antichrist Superstar" faced significant censorship attempts, with an important portion being cut. Some of this censored audiovisual material only began to surface years later, around 2005-2007, often released by the video clip creators rather than Marilyn Manson himself. "hubo una parte importante que acabó siendo censurada y que era bastante señores más tarde, sobre todo, ya avanzados en el 2005, 2006, 2007, es como que han ido saliendo, poco a poco no ya por Mey Manson sino por el trabajador del video clip y todo."

srcs.episode: Cómo Marilyn Manson revolucionó el mundo con Antichrist Superstar

podcast.body: The production of "Antichrist Superstar" was an "absolute lack of control," pushing all participants to physical extremes. Marilyn Manson and Trent Reznor worked to their physical and psychological limits for a year, with Manson especially pushed during idea development. Extreme methods included manipulating and destroying recording tapes, and playing partially destroyed instruments to achieve specific sonic deterioration. "fue una absoluta falta de control en la que todas las personas que formaron parte llegaron a los extremos físicos de no poder soportarlo para llegar a trabajar el disco."

srcs.episode: Cómo Marilyn Manson revolucionó el mundo con Antichrist Superstar

podcast.body: This album is considered one of the most important and captivating works in the history of rock and possibly music in general. It is a profoundly philosophical album, drawing significant inspiration from the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, particularly his works *The Antichrist*, *Ecce Homo*, and *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*. The album's title itself is inspired by Nietzsche's *The Antichrist* and the film *Jesus Christ Superstar*. Manson uses religion, especially Christianity, to exemplify societal problems and philosophical dilemmas, viewing religion as a means of morally constraining individuals. The album is structured into three acts, mirroring Nietzsche's three phases of human liberation, but reinterpreted by Manson in a darker and more macabre way. It features continuous references to Christianity and Judaism, with inspirations from the Jewish Kabbalah appearing in its booklet. Despite often being simplistically viewed as an attack on religion, it is a complex philosophical piece that also critiques law, police, state, and government structures. "es uno de los discos más importantes y apasionantes que jamás se han hecho."

podcast.body: This album propelled Marilyn Manson directly into the mainstream, transforming him into an unstoppable force. It garnered numerous awards not only for the album itself but also for its controversial music videos, solidifying his commercial and critical success. "Meli Manzon da el salto directo al mainstream y se convierte en una máquina imparable, recibió muchísimos premios por este disco, incluso por el videoquilip de Anticristos, sobre esta recibió muchísimos premios."

srcs.episode: Cómo Marilyn Manson revolucionó el mundo con Antichrist Superstar

podcast.body: Upon its release, "Antichrist Superstar" divided some listeners as Marilyn Manson delved deeper into industrial rock sounds, reminiscent of Nine Inch Nails, moving away from the intense hard rock or dark metal of their earlier works, resulting in a sound much more aligned with Trent Reznor's style. "Mey Manson se adentra más en sonidos, pues a lo mejor del rock industrial de Nine Inch Nays, dejando a lo mejor ese rock o ese dar metal tan intenso que tenían las primeras partes aquí por si lo entes ya como más industriales como un sonido como mucho más tren Retnorm."
